title: How to Have a Hard Conversation
excerpt: The conversation you keep avoiding is usually the one that would heal the thing. Avoidance is not peace. It is just slower damage.
body:
There is a conversation you are avoiding right now. You know the one. The thing you need to say to your spouse, your friend, your boss, your parent, that you keep not saying because saying it feels dangerous and not saying it feels safe. Here is the hard truth I have had to learn over and over in fifteen years of ministry: the not saying is not safe. Avoidance does not prevent the damage. It just spreads it out over a longer time, lets it grow in the dark, and turns a hard conversation now into a much harder one later, or a quiet death of the relationship that never gets a chance to heal. Jesus did not say blessed are the conflict-avoiders. He said blessed are the peacemakers (Matthew 5:9), and peacemaking is active, not the absence of trouble.

## Go directly, and go alone first

When someone has wronged you, Jesus is specific about the order of operations. Go and tell him his fault, between you and him alone (Matthew 18:15). Alone first. Not to the group chat, not to your other friends, not to everyone except the actual person. We reverse this constantly. We tell everyone but the one who could fix it, which is not addressing the problem, it is just spreading it while looking like we care.

Going directly is harder and far kinder. It gives the person a chance to respond, to explain, to repent, that they never get when you talk around them instead of to them. So before you have the hard conversation in your head with everyone else, have the real one with the person who is actually in it.

## Aim for restoration, not for winning

Before you open your mouth, get your goal straight, because it will leak into every word. If your goal is to win, to be proven right, to make them feel as bad as they made you feel, the conversation will become a battle and you will probably get the fight you came for. If your goal is to restore, to understand and be understood and make the relationship right, you will speak differently.

The aim that Scripture sets is restoration, gently (Galatians 6:1), not victory. This is not weakness. It is harder than fighting, because it means staying soft toward someone who has hurt you. But a conversation aimed at restoration can heal things a conversation aimed at winning will only deepen. Decide your goal before you decide your words.

## Say the true thing kindly, and own your part

Two failures wreck hard conversations. One is honesty without love, the truth delivered like a weapon, accurate and cruel. The other is love without honesty, so much softening and hedging that the actual point never lands and nothing changes. The target is truth in love (Ephesians 4:15), both at once: the real thing said, and said with care.

Use plain words. Speak for yourself, what you saw, what it did to you, rather than narrating their motives, which you cannot actually see. And own your part early. There is almost always a part. Going in with a confession of your own contribution, before you name theirs, disarms the defensiveness that would otherwise eat the whole conversation. The log in your own eye comes first (Matthew 7:5), and naming it first is not just righteous, it is wise.

## Listen like you might be missing something

A hard conversation is not a speech you deliver. It is an exchange, and if you have already scripted their lines and your rebuttals, you are not having a conversation, you are staging a performance with a hostage. Go in genuinely open to learning that you saw it wrong, or partly wrong, because you often have.

Be quick to hear and slow to speak (James 1:19). Ask what you are missing. Let them finish without loading your reply while they talk. People can feel the difference between being heard and being waited out, and almost nothing softens a hard conversation faster than the other person realizing you are actually listening rather than just reloading.

## This week

Name the conversation you have been avoiding, and the person it belongs to. Go to that person directly, this week, alone first. Before you speak, decide that your goal is to restore, not to win, and start by owning your part.

The conversation you dread is usually the one that would heal the thing. Avoidance feels like peace and is only delay. Go and have it, gently, and in the open.
